paragraphs.text: Blue-black ( or UB ), also called Dimir , is an allied color pair. Blue ( ) and black ( ) share a philosophy of choice; they are mutual enemies of green ( ), the color of destiny. Blue and black have little mechanical overlap, but they both use the evergreen keywords flash and flying , and they are the foremost colors of mill , saboteur effects, and playing opponents' cards. Blue-black decks tend to win by gaining subtle card advantage over time.

Blue seeks knowledge, and black seeks power. They are mutual enemies of green , which believes that everyone's role in life is predetermined. The blue-black alliance is therefore about choice. Blue is adaptable and rational, while black is ruthless and opportunistic; both colors believe in their ability to choose their own path.

When paired, blue and black seek to reshape the world for their own selfish ends. Blue-black is the most ruthless color pair, unhampered by emotions or morality; premeditated murder is quintessentially blue-black. It is secretive and stealthy, hoarding knowledge as a form of power while obfuscating the truth from others; blackmail is an example of blue-black's willingness to exploit information. And it is intelligent, only taking actions that further its long-term plans. Blue-black is also the loneliest color pair; believing the worst of others, it lives in a state of constant fear. It also lacks spontaneity; it has trouble dealing with situations that it hasn't studied and prepared for. And it is slow, although not as slow as white-blue .

Blue and black's disagreements mirror the white-red conflict : security versus freedom. Blue, an ally of white , opposes chaos and disorder, so it wants society to keep unruly individuals in check. Black, an ally of red , chafes against rules that limit its own actions. Blue is also slow and methodical in its decision-making, while black is more willing to act in the moment.
Examples of blue-black heroes include Nashi and Kaito Shizuki , while villains include Szadek and Silumgar .

Blue-black has the least mechanical overlap of any color pair, making it the hardest to design cards for. This is especially true of hybrid ( ) cards. But even gold cards can be difficult to design because technically distinct effects feel similar. For example, blue can draw cards without restriction, while black can only draw cards by paying some additional cost, so it's hard to design a draw spell that feels simultaneously blue and black. Still, they do share some effects, including mill , evasion , and saboteur abilities. And gold cards can sometimes combine the two colors' effects in novel ways, as with Recoil .

Blue-black doesn't lend itself to an obvious archetype or game plan. Instead, blue-black decks tend to win through the subtle accumulation of card advantage , often in ways that inexperienced players might not realize. This mirrors blue-black's philosophy as the sneakiest color pair. Other paths to victory can include mill and evasive creatures.
The following mechanics are shared by blue and black.
These multicolored cards best exemplify the strengths of blue and black:
Recoil — Black's discard ability combined with blue's ability to bounce permanents
Sleeper's Robe — Black's fear ability combined with blue's card-drawing ability
Blizzard Specter — Black's ability to disrupt a player's hand and blue's ability to bounce permanents
